zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after independent scan reading: the supplied National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics (NINJAL) Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510 (Hideyuki Ohshima; assisting developer Taichi Aida), licensed CC BY 4.0, https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html. The diplomatic readings and English notes here are reviewer-authored; this index does not determine the copy’s spelling or typography.

lines.note: Tǒji is explained by ima no toki, the present time. The scan has a single initial T, not the OCR’s Tr; the Portuguese phrase continues with preſente below.
Completes esta hora preſente, making explicit that this first Tǒji entry concerns the present moment.
This homophonous Tǒji means this monastery or temple. The Portuguese contrasts its institutional sense with the preceding temporal entry; the historical word varela is retained.

runs.text: Miolo de junco, que ſerue de torcida.

lines.note: Tôjimi denotes the pith of rush used as a lamp wick. The abraded initial retains the top and stem of T, matching the surrounding headwords, rather than OCR F.

Tǒjin is paraphrased as Kara no hito, a person from China. The enlarged mark is a caron like that of the next entry, correcting the OCR’s circumflex; the Portuguese gives the same national designation.
This Tǒjin is equated with nusubito and glossed as a thief. The visible capital N and following u correct the malformed OCR Xuſubito.
Tojiqimi and the alternative shikii designate a threshold. The damaged first vowel is read as o; the Portuguese begins a description of the timber crossing the doorway.
Completes portal da porta em baixo: the threshold timber lies across the bottom of the door opening.
Tôjit is explained by fuyu no hi, a winter day. Fuyuno has one initial F followed directly by u; the OCR’s extra i is unsupported.
The Japanese explanation invokes fighting and contention, with kenka as a synonym. The scan supports Tatacai, not Tatatai; the Portuguese arroi- continues into arroido below.
Completes arroido and adds briga, a quarrel or fight. This is the continuation of the contention entry rather than a separate item.
This Tǒjǒ denotes this fortress. It is a separate entry from the preceding word for contention and the following act of ascending to a castle.

Shiro ni noboru explains ascending or going up to a fortress. The first accent is badly abraded, but its surviving roof-shaped trace supports ô rather than the preceding entry’s ǒ; the supplied NINJAL index also distinguishes these two headwords. This faint mark remains a nonblocking reading caveat.
Tojǒ denotes the innermost enclosure or castle, with houses mentioned across the break. The missing e in OCR castllo is visible in castello; the unspaced Aderradeira is retained.

runs.text: ſas que eſtão dentro da fortaleza.

lines.note: Completes caſas and places those houses within the fortress. The row remains part of the enclosure definition.
Tǒjǔ is explained by answering or responding, with Portuguese repoſta. The headword ends in marked u without the OCR’s extra i; the next sense concerns correspondence.

runs.text: Palaura q̃ ſe poem nos ſobreſcritos das cartas

lines.note: The second sense concerns a word placed in the superscriptions of letters. The abbreviation q̃ is preserved without expansion; its relative clause continues below.

runs.text: que vão em repoſta de outras.

lines.note: The letters are replies to earlier letters, explaining the correspondence use of Tǒjǔ. The damaged final letter of vão is a rounded o, not OCR y; S. is the upright written-register label.
This separate Tǒjǔ is grape wine, paraphrased as budō no shiru. The abraded u of Budǒno is supported by the surviving strokes and grape-wine gloss; S. marks written usage.

runs.text: Esteira que ſe vſa pera emparo da chu-

lines.note: Toma is a mat used for shelter from rain. The scan supports contiguous Esteira rather than OCR Este ra; the gloss’s rain word is divided chu- / ua.

runs.text: ua nas embarcações, ou noutras partes.

lines.note: Completes chuua and specifies use on vessels or elsewhere. This is the continuation of the rain-covering mat definition.
Toma wo fuku means covering or roofing with mats, here applied to a boat. The paragraph mark before the Japanese example is visible and was omitted by OCR.
Completes the description of covering a vessel with these mats. The scan reads esteiras, not the OCR’s estriras; the source’s st form is retained.

Tomabuki denotes covering with toma mats; the example uses tomabuki ni suru. The damaged headword b and example n are read from the remaining strokes and the repeated form, correcting Tonabuqi and Tomabuqiri. The example’s n is abraded, so Tomabuqini is retained as a chosen but qualified reading.

runs.text: aßi de empreſtado algũa caſa, ou outra couſa

lines.note: The Portuguese describes a makeshift covering for a house or another object. Outra includes the visible t omitted in OCR oura; the tilde remains over u in algũa.
Completes the temporary-roofing definition with these straw mats. The two words estas and eſteiras retain their supplied allographic distinction.

Tǒmachicu-i names rice, hemp, bamboo and reeds, as the four Japanese glosses show. The hyphen and final i belong to the headword; Ine is the rice word, not OCR Ite. The Portuguese palavra is physically divided without a securely visible end hyphen.

runs.text: laura pera declarar que vem, ou estão muitos

lines.note: Completes palavra and explains that this expression describes many people arriving or standing together. The scan supports laura and vem, not the malformed OCR liura and vemn.

runs.text: homẽs juntos, particularmente quando eſtão com

lines.note: Specifies men gathered together, particularly when bearing weapons. Homẽs has an initial h, not OCR b, and retains its abbreviation tilde.
The men have their weapons and spears raised. Aleuantadas is one word in the scan, replacing OCR ales aita ſas; the next Japanese example begins with the divided headword.

runs.text: chicu-ino gotoqu yari, nagui natauo ta-

lines.note: Completes Tǒmachicu-i no gotoku and compares upright spears and naginata with densely growing plants. The scan supports an i after nagu; its visible gap before natauo is retained instead of joining the form editorially.

Terareta completes the Japanese verb for erecting the weapons. The Portuguese says they had raised the spears and naginata; Tinhão is wholly Portuguese italic text, and the divided Na begins the Japanese weapon name within that explanation.

runs.text: guinatas à maneira de ſementeira de arroz eſ-

lines.note: Guinatas completes the divided weapon name Naguinatas. The explanation compares the raised weapons with a field of rice; the final eſ- belongs to eſpigado on the next row.
Completes eſpigado and lists flax/hemp, bamboo and reeds as the plants evoked by the dense array of weapons. The printed canemo is retained without supplying a modern accent.
Crecidos completes the description of the tall or grown plants. This short line closes the Tǒmachicu-i entry.
Tǒmame is glossed as broad beans. The initial T is abraded but its remaining vertical stroke is visible; it must not be dropped as in the OCR.

runs.text: Detença, ou porto pera ſurgirem as

lines.note: Tomari denotes a stopping place or harbour where vessels anchor. The Portuguese verb surgir has its nautical sense here, completed by embarcações below.
The vessels are the subject of ſurgirem in the preceding row, completing the harbour definition.
The principal forms tomari, tomaru, tomatta describe stopping, resting or remaining. The initial T matches the other headwords and corrects OCR Fomari.
Tori ga ki no eda ni tomaru describes a bird perching on a tree branch. The initial t of tomaru is damaged but agrees with the headword and its visible type; comaru would be a different verb.

runs.text: deterſe o paßaro no ramo daruore. ¶

lines.note: Completes the bird-perching translation, then starts a new example with dangui, a sermon or discourse. The historical daruore spelling remains unchanged.
The object particle continues Dangui: although hearing a sermon, nothing stays in the ears. Tomaranu is the negative of the same verb, used figuratively for retention.

runs.text: Ainda q̃ ouço pregação não me fica nada nos

lines.note: Begins the Portuguese translation: although I hear preaching, nothing remains in my ears. The opening vowel of ouço is o, not OCR c, while q̃ remains abbreviated.
Completes the ears phrase and introduces the further sense of an activity ceasing. Co- starts the next example’s kono across the physical break.

runs.text: no cuni ranno vchinareba, ranbuto, cha-

lines.note: Kono kuni ran no uchi nareba sets the example amid turmoil in the country. The scan supports vchinareba rather than the OCR’s vehinarebi; ranbu and the divided chanoyu expression name the activities that stop.

Completes chanoyu-zuki and says that these pursuits stopped abruptly. Mon. is a roman citation label; the Portuguese translation begins Aue- / do. An abbreviation tilde over e is not securely established in this worn impression, so the supplied unmarked Aue- is retained without supplying the expected n.

runs.text: do neste reino reuoltas, & perturbações ceßa-

lines.note: The translation describes upheavals and disturbances in the kingdom, after which the activities ceased. The scan has do and perturbações, correcting OCR de and perurbações; ceßa- continues as rão at the next column’s top.

runs.text: rão derepente os bailos, tangeres, & cantos,

lines.note: Rão completes ceßa- at the foot of the first column. The translation lists dances, instrumental music and singing as activities that ceased; the visible b corrects OCR hailos.

Adds the practice of chanoyu to the suspended activities. Enlargement shows the initial c at the lowercase body height; chanoyu is a Japanese cultural term within the Portuguese explanation and is identified for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: Gallinha, ou gallo da China, que he

lines.note: Tǒmaru denotes a Chinese hen or cock. The definition’s comparison with Japanese fowl continues on the next line.

runs.text: mayor, & mais forte que o de Iapão.

lines.note: Completes the poultry description as larger and stronger than the Japanese kind. The historical Portuguese mayor is preserved.
Tǒmat contrasts ima and sue, present and future. The terminal fu- begins futuro, with a visible f rather than OCR long s; the final t of the Japanese headword is retained.
Completes futuro and paraphrases the contrast as now and later. Tǒmatno begins the Japanese example, with the attached genitive particle preserved.
Shian ga iru means that consideration is necessary, here of present and future circumstances. The scan supports conſiderar, restoring the i omitted by OCR.
Completes preſente and the paired future, closing the example’s Portuguese translation.
Tomaya is explained as a toma house, covered with straw mats. The Portuguese certas is divided across this row and the next.

runs.text: tas esteiras de palha, ou pobre, & baixa.

lines.note: Completes certas esteiras de palha and adds that the house is humble and low. This is a description of the same dwelling, not a separate headword.
The principal forms tome, tomuru, tometa mean stopping or detaining a person or thing. The end mark following al is retained provisionally as the supplied point; the word continues below.
Completes algũa couſa, extending the transitive stopping verb to an object as well as a person. The tilde stays on u as printed.

runs.text: Agulha que ſe mete em certa par-

lines.note: Tomebari denotes a needle inserted into a particular part of the body. The Portuguese explanation describes a therapeutic use, continued on the next row.

runs.text: te do corpo pera impedir as camaras. ¶

lines.note: The stated purpose is to stop diarrhoeal evacuations, the historical sense of camaras here. The next example repeats the needle term across the line break.
Completes tomebari wo tatsuru, setting or administering this needle. The Portuguese repeats the action as giving the needle puncture.

runs.text: ¶ Item, O arrematar a costura. Vt,

lines.note: A second sense concerns fastening off a seam. The scan supports costura, with damaged o rather than OCR a; To- begins the sewing example below.
Completes tomebari wo suru, performing the fastening-off stitch. This Japanese example belongs to the second, sewing-related sense rather than the preceding therapeutic needle.

runs.text: Lugar, ou modo de ter, ou fa-

lines.note: Tomedokoro is a place or means of stopping or restraining. The Portuguese fazer is divided at the line end and continues below.
Completes fazer ceßar, then gives a person with no stopping point or means of restraint. The following translation develops the unrestrained-person example.

runs.text: Homem que não ha podelo ter, nem fazer ceſ-

lines.note: The person cannot be restrained or made to stop. The Portuguese infinitive ceſſar is divided between the two long-s forms across this physical line boundary.

runs.text: ſar na pratica, ou noutra couſa que vai conti-

lines.note: Completes ceſſar and applies the lack of restraint to conversation or another continued activity. Pratica has its speech/conversation sense here.
Completes continuando and closes the explanation of someone who goes on without stopping.
Tomeyama is a reserved or closed woodland or mountain. The Portuguese comparison with a protected preserve continues on the next row.
Coutada completes the reserved-land comparison, clarifying that access or use is restricted.
Tomi, tomu means being rich or prospering. The source labels it Verbo defect.; that grammatical qualification is preserved without inventing omitted principal parts.
Completes proſpero and adds the verb proſperar. The paired gloss describes both the state of wealth and becoming prosperous.
Tômiǒ denotes a devotional lamp, with miyakashi as its Japanese synonym. The scan shows a capital M, correcting OCR Xiyacaxi; the lamp word alampada is divided across rows.

runs.text: da que ſe poem diante do Fotoque, ou Camis.

lines.note: Completes alampada and places the lamp before the Buddha or kami. Fotoque and Camis are Japanese terms embedded in the Portuguese explanation and are identified for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: As vezes ſe toma pello azeite, ou cera que

lines.note: The term may also designate the oil or wax itself. This metonymic extension of the lamp name continues into the burning-fuel clause below.
The oil or wax burns before the image. Idolo is the Portuguese gloss’s religious terminology and is retained as part of the historical source.
Tomisakaye denotes prospering or flourishing in wealth. The Japanese principal forms and Portuguese flourishing verb both continue the semantic field of tomi.
Completes florecer em riquezas, specifying material prosperity rather than literal flowering.

runs.text: Companhia, ou os que a companhão.

lines.note: Tomo denotes company or the people accompanying someone. The source’s separation a companhão is retained, without modernizing it to a single Portuguese word.
Otomo ni mairō is the deferential offer to accompany someone. The Portuguese begins I shall go with you, continuing with a more respectful form of address below.

runs.text: com voßa mercè. ¶ Item, Moços, ou cri-

lines.note: Completes the respectful address voßa mercè, correcting OCR voßia. A further sense describes boys or servants, with criados divided across the line break.

runs.text: ados que acompanhão aſeu amo. Vt,

lines.note: Completes criados and specifies servants accompanying their master. To- begins the verbal example tomo suru on the next physical line.

runs.text: A companhar o moço aſeu amo.

lines.note: Completes tomo suru, a servant accompanying his master. The Portuguese initial A companhar preserves the printed spacing rather than silently joining it.
Tomo no shū denotes companions or an accompanying group. The damaged capital T is visible, replacing the OCR’s long-s initial in ſomono.
Completes the group description: people who accompany someone. The visible a companha spacing is preserved.
This separate tomo means the stern of a vessel. It is a nautical noun, unrelated to the preceding companion sense in this entry sequence.
This tomo is concessive, glossed as even if or granted that. Fito- begins the example with hito on the following line.
Completes hito naritomo, even if he is a man. The Portuguese explicitly supplies the concessive sense of the preceding entry.

runs.text: Como quer que ſeja, ou de qual

lines.note: Tomokakumo means however it may be or in whatever manner. The scan has distinct word gaps in quer que ſeja and the final l of qual; no terminal hyphen is supplied before quer below.
Quer completes qualquer across the physical break, followed by any manner whatsoever. It is part of the preceding gloss, not a new word entry.
Tomo kōmo receives the same meaning as tomokakumo. The initial is a capital T with a damaged top, not OCR r; the caron on cǒmo is retained.
This compound names a hood or cap open at the top. The doubled z in zzuqin is retained as the source’s Japanese spelling, and the gloss explains the unusual construction below.

runs.text: de maneira que ſe pode por na cabeça por am-

lines.note: The cap can be put onto the head through either opening. The last am- begins ambas on the following row.
Completes ambas as aberturas and closes the cap definition. The separate Tomo- at the far right is a catchword anticipating Tomodachi on the next page, not part of this body line.
